1.t: The spirited, laid-back second-line beat after the burial
1.s: After the burial the bands played funky, unhurried music with big bass drum figures by Black Benny and Ernest Trepagnier, a celebration of a life lived out.
1.q: Raunchy. [Barker sings a melody.] On the bass drum Black Benny or Ernest Trepagnier. Great bass drum beaters. They be hitting that drum, and them figures in the snare drums and the rim shots. They don’t do that no more. See the rhythm section would be there right in the middle of the band, see?…

1.t: Jazz funeral ceremony and cutting the body loose
1.s: Barker describes dirges on the way to the cemetery, turning the body loose, the switch to Didn't He Ramble, and the idea that Black mourners were going to glory.
1.q: They play those dirges. Flee as a Bird, What a Friend We Have in Jesus, if it was solemn. Some people didn’t want no inspired, in fact they didn’t play no spirited music until they turned the body loose. That’s what they call the turning loose. You know what that is.

1.t: Military funerals for whites versus jazz funerals
1.s: White New Orleanians had military funerals, and the visiting service bands Barker followed did not know how to swing out.
1.q: No, they never . . . They had military funerals for whites. If he was a general in the army, or he was a navy man, or he belonged to one these artillery . . . They had a whole lot of artillery, batallion societies that they kept going all the time. Different branches of service. The brigade. They…

1.t: Grandfather Barbarin, the hearse driver Joe Never Smile
1.s: His grandfather played mellophone and alto horn, drove carriages and hearses, and never smiled or moved at funerals.
1.ch: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
1.q: Mellophone and alto horn. He had played trumpet to begin with, but they told him to get off the trumpet. But he was just about as Creole as you could get. He used to eat dinner every day at 12 o'clock with his bottle of wine. He was French as you... He'd never say nothin'. He never said nothing,…

1.t: Why New Orleans swung, and Dejan's band at Paul Barbarin's funeral
1.s: He ties swinging to party dancing, complains that Harold Dejan's band played swinging music with the family present at Paul Barbarin's funeral, and tells the history of the church.
1.ch: The banjo, rhythm and the New Orleans style
1.q: All right. That church. He was laid out in there. They were surprised how they laid him out in the church. Well his grandmother gave the first dollar to the priest that opened that church. Came to the neighborhood and said they need a church here. “Would you all help me? I’m going to start picking…

1.t: NBC News report on Armstrong's funeral in Queens
1.s: Wilson Hall reports the funeral service, the minister's eulogy, hymns by Al Hibbler, Peggy Lee and Hugh Porter, and Fred Robbins's tribute to Armstrong's life and influence.
1.q: This is NBC News. Goodbye, Louis, King of Jazz. This is Wilson Hall. Louis Sachmo Armstrong, jazz trumpeter, was buried today near the Queens, New York home, where he had lived for 30 years. The funeral service was held in a small, simple, red-brick congregational church in Armstrong's…

306.t: Playing after the funeral and changing attitudes about funeral music
306.s: Rene recalls bands playing lively ramble numbers after burial, and says people are now cautious about offending families.
306.q: Oh yeah, well, yes, but it is. Well all the bands used to play it, because most of the fellas, they used to play, they all used to ramble. See? They all would see the good time or you know, a little bit of shit. They'd do something, they would smile some way or another. But all the bands had that…

306.t: A honeymoon brass band story and changing funeral times and habits
306.s: Zander recounts an airport honeymoon brass band. Rene notes funerals once held at 1 or 2 pm are now at any hour, and musicians' lives have changed.
306.q: Well, another thing too about, one thing about funeral is too, you better funeral is not, if you wanted a band at that time, you wouldn't have that if you're funeral that would be around 2 o'clock, 1 o'clock. I noticed they had bands around you in the morning, no, they didn't do that a long time…

306.t: Second-line clapping and funeral music's emotional pull
306.s: They agree funeral players still play for fun and the second line's clapping gives rhythm; Rene sees funeral traditions spreading.
306.q: Oh, yeah, well, you see, they got, they get, well, they got a kick out, you see, because that second line keep them emotional, you know. That second line keep them fellas happy, because them fellas out there clapping, and they're giving them a rhythm. That second line gives them a rhythm sometimes…

306.s: Edna describes the huge funeral with seven bands and says Chris died at Lincoln Bell, which she links to drinking.
306.q: Oh, everybody. White and colored. Everybody. White and colored. Everybody. He had a funeral. It was long, it was from where I'm sitting, almost to Espinay Street. Yes. But the rain came out and there was, the people was willing to walk with the bands. He had seven bands volunteered behind. Where…

306.t: Old burial jewelry, cemetery fights and the huge second line for Black Benny
306.s: Rene recalls people buried with jewelry, fights after funerals between uptown and downtown, and a ten-block-long funeral with second liners dancing on both sides.
306.q: That's right. All that was requested, he wanted to be full dressed. And see, a long time ago when they used to bury people, they used to bury people with all their jewelry. They were watching everything, everything a person desired, they were buried, you see. That's why you take the section, the…

306.t: Wives at funerals and tipping the bandleader for tunes
306.s: Rene describes a wife and an outside wife at funerals and how mourners tipped the bandleader to play pointed songs.
306.q: She might be way back. And if they don't know, well then, stay, they, if they ain't got enough room, the family need more room, well, she might try to squeeze in there. You know what I'm saying? If they don't know anything was going on, she would squeeze in there, but she knows something's going…

181.t: Funeral music and the second line
181.s: Parker explains reading music, ragtime coming back from funerals and the second line; trouble at funerals.
181.ch: Mac, railroads and the second line
181.q: Music is, we used to get our music from one line, you know? And music is simple. One, two, three, five lines and four spaces. See, that's music. A fella come to you right now and say, you miss this thing? I say, what is music? Well, some fellas can't tell him, cause they wasn't taught to. The…

181.s: Parker loved funerals, played in the Terminal brass band; no funerals in the country; big societies had two bands.
181.q: No, ma'am. No, ma'am. They didn't. They didn't use no funerals in the country at that time.

181.s: Mac explains Catholic parishes and crepe, black and second mourning.
181.ch: Church funerals, band size and mourning
181.q: And then they'd get out there and get in the second morning.

181.t: Societies, women's funerals and an Indian-suit burial
181.s: Societies, no band funerals for women, and a woman buried in an Indian suit; Muddy's church downtown.
181.q: Well, the fellow that killed her, he's out. Yeah, he been out. He's been out a good while. He belongs to Muddy's church.

798.t: Where funeral processions assemble and where the body lies
798.s: Clark explains bands meet at the society hall or a corner, and bodies are at the church or undertaker, often after a wake, especially in Algiers.
798.q: See, some of them meet different places. See, like over there they meet, over there, that hall over there, like up here they meet up there. Wherever they meet, they disband, they go and make a human disband in the same place. Would it always be a hall? Well, mostly, yeah.

798.t: Counting funerals per year; other bands' funeral work
798.s: Clark counts about twenty funerals this year and about thirteen in 1956; they discuss John Kazimer and George Williams.
798.q: That's last year. It looks about the same. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen. That's last year. It's 56. This is the year right after she died. That's one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve. Twelve and it all rests…

798.s: Clark says he has played for women of high rank in orders like the Eastern Star, with the same music as for men.
798.q: Well, you see, you take these women that hold these high orders in the Eastern Star, cultural ampers, and all the big high positions in there where they give them music. Sure.

304.t: Jazz funerals today, orderly second lines and umbrellas
304.s: They discuss funerals for musicians, Wood never saw second lines unruly or fights, and contrasts tattered umbrellas then with fancy ones now.
304.ch: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
304.q: They were always on the sidewalk, close to the band, you know, up next to it. They would surge back and forth, but I've never seen them get unruly and I've never seen them really interfere in any way with the procession itself, the progress of the thing.

304.t: Funeral music, the marshal and John Casimir's tears
304.s: Funeral bands switched from fast warm-up numbers to slow marches, the marshal set the mood, and Casimir wept while playing clarinet.
304.ch: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
304.q: But that was always a striking and exciting thing is when at a funeral, and I really didn't go to a lot of funerals, maybe three or four, maybe a couple more, but that they would play that, the band and the club that was the deceased had been a member of, they would assemble somewhere a couple of…

304.t: Waiting outside funerals; never following to the cemetery
304.s: Wood fraternized with musicians over beer while services ran, and never followed a funeral into the cemetery.
304.ch: Funerals, second lines and being an outsider
304.q: And I used to, uh, when they were going to funerals, uh, when the procession would get in the church and they would have that part of it, the preaching and the singing of the choir. Yeah. The band would frequently just be sitting around outside waiting for them to come out. Mm-hmm. And, uh, you…

696.t: Explaining the second line and the music at a jazz funeral
696.s: Dirges on the way to the grave, lively tunes after, the family as first line and onlookers as second line; religion makes no difference outside the church.
696.q: Yeah. When a person passes, when they die, the tradition is the jazz funeral in which the family — we have a procession that goes to the gravesite and there’s a brass band that’s playing, what we call dirges, which is a slow, very slow song, it’s moving, very slow and very solemn-like. It’s not the…

696.t: Preparing to play funerals; music as a celebration of life
696.s: A New Orleans musician prepares from birth; music's purpose is to celebrate life, not to get sidetracked by industry.
696.q: How do you prepare? Well I guess you prepare if you’re born and raised in New Orleans from the time that you come into this life you’re preparing yourself. It’s not something that all of a sudden happens. It’s just a way of life. It’s like the breath. It’s in the way you walk, the way you speak,…

696.t: What New Orleans jazz funerals mean, and the funeral of Waldron 'Frog' Joseph
696.s: Musicians and mourners from all walks of life set differences aside at jazz funerals; he recalls the funeral of trombonist Waldron 'Frog' Joseph.
696.q: Yeah, yeah. From all walks of life you know. If you’ve ever been to New Orleans and attended a jazz funeral in New Orleans, you know like some of the old time jazz musicians, when they pass, it’s always at that time when I attend one of those and I listen to the music, I listen to the musicians…

98.t: Elgar's death and New Orleans funeral in Chicago
98.s: Elgar died at 94; Saunders, executor of his estate, gave him a New Orleans funeral with Jean Carroll singing, which the Tribune ignored.
98.ch: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
98.q: Yeah, he was still acting and he was teaching and then his hearing kind of went. He was 94 years old when he died, and we gave him a New Orleans funeral. I was the executor to his -- for his estate.

98.t: Community advice and a New Orleans funeral concert in a funeral parlor
98.s: His phone is an advice center; he also did a Shrove Tuesday New Orleans funeral concert with Franz Jackson.
98.ch: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
98.q: Right, I told about it. Well, anyway, -- and we had the New Orleans thing and we did the whole bit about New Orleans. And we did the funeral things. Franz Jackson was there and he -- and "Didn't He Ramble" on the way back from the funeral and all of that. It was beautiful, and they enjoyed it so…

98.t: Chester Chapp (Trader Horn) plans his own jazz funeral
98.s: A rattan shop owner and music lover who ordered a band for his funeral and a party at a Greek restaurant.
98.ch: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
98.q: Now, talking about strange things that happen to people. I don't know whether you remember this fellow, he had a basket shop up on North State Street.

862.t: Turning the band loose at distant funerals
862.s: With far cemeteries, bands play through the procession, split and play for the funeral passing, then return to the hall.
862.q: Well, we'd go through the distance, so we'd get to the corner there and stand and divide ourselves, open up, you understand, and play what the funerals would be going through, you see. And then after they'd gone through, well, we'd come on back to the hall.

862.t: From church to cemetery and back to the hall
862.s: What happens at the cemetery, the route back to the society hall, and the music played returning. Musicians feed themselves.
862.q: In the cemetery, you place a hand, you know, or a few of them. A few of them, a few of them, a kind of a short, you understand? And then after the pretty minute tour, or after you beat them somewhere there, when you finish. You know, you know, you're a place where you're a little piece of open, you…

430.t: Funeral hearse, black horses and horse shrouds
430.s: The old horse-drawn hearse, its decorations, the black shrouds on the horses and what they cost.
430.q: I mean... Oh, no. They didn't have... They had... No, it's time. I mean, they had the hoist with two black horses, I mean.

430.t: Funeral tunes: Didn't He Ramble, hymns and Bourbon Street Parade
430.s: Which pieces were appropriate on the way to and from the cemetery, and the idea of recording a real brass band.
430.q: Well the first thing they used to play, when they used to turn the body loose, before, I mean years ago, it would be Denny Ramble. Denny Ramble. That's the first thing they did. They wouldn't be twenty-five feet from the cemetery before Denny Ramble. Denny Ramble. Denny Ramble. Denny Ramble.

773.t: Black Benny, drummer, and his death
773.s: Black Benny's drums, a cornerstone laying trip, his being stabbed that night, and her unease about funerals.
773.q: He played, he played, he played a bass drum and then he had them little, what you call them, tambourines that hit on, they played that too. Then he had them sags you hit on the drum, you know, like little brooms, you know. He played that. He was a great musician, you know. And we went to a…

773.t: Second liners and the meaning of New Orleans funerals
773.s: Arnold Jr. describes the Original Second Liners, collections, slow hymns to the grave and lively music after.
773.q: Wait ma. Oh, excuse me. And the police shot this little guy. Then it all happened in this area around the Calzone. Get him, Lou. They even have a club they call the original Second Liners. I don't know if you noticed when they have a band, a guy called it with Banner. And they're supposed to be…

626.t: How the band played funeral marches and the return from the cemetery
626.s: He describes society funerals: slow hymns, muffled snare drums, and livelier tunes like So Glad You're Gone on the way back.
626.q: No, they made it to society's hall. Then we just marched with the drum to the corpse house or wherever they were laid out at. March there with the drum. Well, they'd play a few church hymns in a slow way, you know, when the corpse was coming out. And after the corpse would come out, we'd get in…

626.t: Funeral crowds, fights and the burial society uniforms
626.s: Big crowds followed funerals, sometimes ending in brick fights; he describes the societies' uniforms and the move of funerals to Sundays.
626.q: Oh yeah, sometimes there's big, big crowds. Sometimes the northern boys, those young stuts, would come from the north, they had a few to come down to the cemetery, the Maynore Cemetery, in the south here. And they'd come down and the big boys would get to fighting and running with bricks and they'd…

627.t: When fife and drum funeral music was heard
627.s: Cage dates the funeral drumming to 1905-1909, with fife and drums, and the interviewer asks what tunes were played.
627.ch: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
627.q: Not much. They used to hear it when they go around these towns.

627.s: Cage says drums were played at funerals, on the way to the cemetery and back.
627.ch: Funerals, societies and the future of fiddling
627.q: They used to beat drums when people died, too. When people died, they beat drums. Yeah, they're nothing.

14.t: Playing a Shreveport veteran's funeral alone for ten dollars
14.s: Love tells how he led a solo cornet funeral procession in Shreveport for a Spanish-American War veteran and joked with the pool-hall musicians afterward.
14.q: Oh yeah, you see, Shreveport, they never had no music for funerals around there at all, but they heard it by New Orleans. A lot of fellas coming down there and they'd see them funerals down there, you know, and some of them would remember. Well, they had a, he was a veteran from the…

14.t: Organizing a 50-piece funeral band for a dead Alexandria musician
14.s: Love tells how Alexandria musicians pooled money for a funeral for a musician killed by a train, and how he conducted the 50-piece band in 1908.
14.q: No, only in New Orleans. But, we built a musician in Alexander, they called him Ollie. Ollie Williams or something like that. He got killed by a train. And the musicians didn't have no union there, but they were all friends, they had a club like, you know. And this was a strange fella he comes out…

873.t: Funeral home phonograph music replacing bands
873.s: Lawrence explains the loudspeaker phonograph used at his funeral home, which people stopped asking for.
873.q: No, I don't know. I do know that an old man, he used to tell me, he said, why don't you all play, learn how to play child music. He said, after a while, you're going to be playing music for a week. And I said, well, I don't believe that. So, we have a funeral home next door there. And then it came…

873.t: Brass bands at funerals and the music coming back
873.s: Bands played for society parades and for deceased band members, with slow pieces going and lively ones coming back along the levee.
873.q: Well, I used to play in the brass band myself, lately, you know. I mean, after we had the string band, we used to play all the parades they had. Every society would have a banquet, they would have a brass band to play, to play the parade, and every member of the band that would die would play the…

836.t: Funeral marches and jazzing on the way back
836.s: Edna and Mr. Senegal describe dead marches on the way to the grave and lively music, "glad you're dead you rascal," after burial.
836.q: Happy. That was at the Catholic Church too? Well, yes, because you see they were away from the church then. They'd buried the dead. The church had nothing to do. The priest was gone. Everybody was gone.

836.t: Her father played tuba in a brass band; his funeral
836.s: Her father played tuba in an all-brass band that played at his funeral when she was 14; they try to recall the band's name.
836.q: Tuva? Tuva. That big thing. The tuva. That's what he played. It was an all brass band that he launched in. That's no string instrument at all. And I remember they played it at his funeral. His members stayed at his funeral in Dallas. And that was history at that time. Oh, everybody. All the bands…

8.t: Wake etiquette, mourning dress and funeral coffins and horses
8.s: Freeloaders at wakes, who paid, why mirrors are covered, mourning clothes, white coffins and horses for the young and black for the old.
8.q: come in there he'd eat you up and go about the business and go look these wakes up you know what do you call them? wakes yeah wakes oh wakes you find uh maybe they had two street to go two of them to go to they made them didn't care where they was out they'd make them last one I can remember a man…

8.t: Wakes: covering mirrors, singing and the open house
8.s: Customs for laying out the dead, the wake with food and drink, a dead woman's eyes moving, and death notices on posts.
8.q: never did they say catapult and never no bound for me no no they see you died and they take the old folks that cover all the pictures they just have pictures all the time on the wall and mirrors well you take a sheet and put it over the mirrors you take a sheet and put it all over the pictures…

643.s: He does not know where the custom came from but recalls the idea of hymns going to the grave and hot music coming back to cheer people.
643.q: I don't know. I wouldn't know. I know it was here all the way it was. And they stopped it because they were so sad, you know. Band would be out there on the grave, on the grave frame, you know, the funeral home. And the relationship would be hard and can't on the dragon. Well, I know it was…

643.t: Funerals with the band, second line, Catholics and Baptists
643.s: They played funerals like New Orleans, with hymns going out and hot music coming back, and played for both Catholic and Baptist societies.
643.q: You think the same over there in Raceland too? Yeah. Yeah, same day all over there. We used to play funerals on that bank. Took the people down to the hotel at the band playing them and come back. Come back, come back, come back, boog in there.

886.s: Step by step what the band plays going to the undertaker, the church and the cemetery, and the rags after the hymn.
886.q: The club and the band are going ready to be, everyone. Mm-hmm. They go to the church, the undertaker to get the body. Go to the undertaker to get the body, and then... Go to the church, you get the care to dismiss it. Mm-hmm. Make the round with that second line, come on in.

886.s: What a brass band plays on a cornerstone-laying line, from the clubhouse to the church to the stone.
886.q: What's on? I want you to play blues and songs and all that. Mm-hmm. I want you to kill out my marching. I want you to want to jump.

782.t: Watching a New Orleans jazz funeral
782.s: He disapproves of tourists at funerals while praising the music of a mixed band.
782.ch: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
782.q: Oh yeah. Actually I think that I shouldn't go there for the first point. I had nothing to do with it, really. I think it's stupid for all the people who are going there, it has nothing to do with it. But I've been there a few times, because Rolf was playing the trumpet in the band. Like on the…

782.t: The Eureka Brass Band and white spectators at funerals
782.s: He recalls hearing Eureka at a funeral across the river and both men dislike white onlookers.
782.ch: Brass bands, funerals and Swedish scene
782.q: Oh yeah. But this is time- he's really hard trying to get this brass band proper I think. Mm-hm. It seems like that- that's why he using bamboo

177.t: Funerals he played and with which bands
177.s: Jiles played funerals with Kid Rene, Chris Kelly, Tuxedo and pickup bands, but never Eureka.
177.q: I played Rene, Kid Rene, played one couple with Chris Kelly, played with the Joan, the Tuxedo band. I never did play any with the Eureka. And I played occasionally make-up bands, Kid Howard, and Chic, and different fellas. A band would have just gone down for that day, Kid Howard band, or Kid Chic.

177.t: Chris Kelly's pickup funeral bands and burial societies
177.s: Kelly had no steady men, and societies once paid for several bands at one funeral.
177.q: No, Chris he, it's like I told you, he didn't have steady men either. Chris would play with you tonight and have a funeral tomorrow and be using somebody else. Because he wasn't a standard, I mean a band that looked forward to a band.

309.t: Organising Cap's funeral and the bells in Mississippi
309.s: Julius and Dick discuss the timing of the deaths, and Julius describes Cap's funeral with band, second line and church bells over the lake.
309.q: Uh, about a year. Because John certainly had a nice send-off. John, his wife, and then he said, about a year and a half between those.

309.t: Sylvester's last request for a second line
309.s: Weeks before he died, Sylvester made Julius promise him a second line, which Julius saw carried out.
309.q: It was something three weeks, three weeks or two and a half weeks before Sylvester passed. He didn't want to eat, and he just thought I should be right there by him. He called me, his wife called me, Jews, I said, yes, she said, Sylvester said, you haven't been out here to see him in a week. She…

0.t: New Orleans funerals as a gimmick
0.s: Dance and Caldwell say the New Orleans funeral band has become a gimmick, and that street funerals have faded in New York.
0.q: "Didn't he they do Ramble." They It's kind of a mockery because it's -- used to play that thing coming back from the funeral-- the "Free as the cemetery, (unintelligible) birds", like that, you know, because we used to -- years ago in New York, had like the big person was -- had died, like Mason or…

0.t: Ray Nance's long funeral and funeral services as shows
0.s: Dance recounts delivering a eulogy at Nance's two-hour funeral and they agree services should not be vaudeville shows.
0.q: I missed Ray Nance -- you know, I didn't know Ray Nance had died until somebody called me on the contemplating Milt Hinton phone, and I was (unintelligible) and this regular Chicago bunch from the south side. The fellow in Denmark said, Hap, all those they get out-of Chicago's together. I said,…

381.t: Marching in St. Agnes band funerals and stopping at the edge of White town
381.s: He describes snares muffled on slow dirges, musicians drinking moonshine during the service, and halting at the boundary of the white section; Hinton notes his nickname Pump.
381.ch: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
381.q: Now, like when St. Agnes's band used to play all these funerals -- we would meet at the hall, at the rehearsal hall where the band used to rehearse at, which was the parish hall of St. Agnes Church. We would meet there, and say, the funeral was going to start at two o'clock -- well, we would meet…

381.t: Wakes and funeral customs in Miami
381.s: The body was brought home the night before the funeral; friends sang hymns, told stories and drank all night.
381.ch: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
381.q: It was the same thing. Like, you know, they used to have at the wake, they would have the wake set, and like if you died, all your friends would come by and different families would cook food.

173.s: Funeral bands, which he associates with Black bands, and Jack Lane, whom he never played with.
173.q: No, I never did. Did you hear his thing? He used to have a lot of scrubs you understand, play with him. I never did see where he had a real band you understand that you could say was everybody played they pause. But he, a noisy fella you see. He used to get the bag, get jobs. He oft times asked me…

248.t: Playing bass drum in parades; brass bands and funerals
248.s: Dawson played bass drum with Edward Clem in Plaquemine; he preferred string and dance music and funerals lacked bands then.
248.q: bass band job i played drum i played the bass drum with uh edward clement in plaquem i played a parade in plaquem and i played bass drum any parades here in town i still got my cymbal beater home there too old cymbal beater my drum beater of the kitchen just as old as it can be but i got in the…

621.s: He explains brass bands played funerals, though he never played in them, and describes the music on the way back from the grave.
621.q: Yes, I, uh, I remember sometimes they did. I don't know if they did at all times. Somebody would, they would go to the... Mm-hm. and when they were coming from the grave, they would play, I'd be glad when you're dead, you rascal you.

479.t: Playing funerals and taps at the grave
479.s: Funerals across the river, marches on the way, lively playing and beer party after.
479.q: Yes. I played funerals. Most of our funerals were played over the river for these fire companies. These volunteer fire companies would have a band. We'd play most of them in Gretchen.

769.s: He describes Benny's killing, his huge funeral with several bands and his bass drum on the hearse, and his reputation as a protector.
769.q: Oh yes, that's where Stella stands. Yeah, Mount Olivet I think he's buried. I think they're taking him as far as Biennival and Galvis. And that's where the bands left the funeral. Take him on out there. But that's where they had his bass drum. I've never seen a funeral for no musician like that…

869.s: Adams describes draped horses and brass bands at funerals but never followed them out of respect.
869.q: brass bands and uh they had old time horses with the horses with the black uh I don't know what you call it all draped down over the horses you know like a mosquito ball all black you know knitted work all the time of the horses had the old brass lamps on each side of the horse old time just like…

241.t: Funerals and parades, and Murray Henderson's huge funeral
241.s: Clubs held parades and two or three funerals a week; Murray Henderson's funeral drew a dozen bands.
241.q: And all that, they got a few now, but them days they had more than that. They used to have parades, men, parade on both sides, and they had plenty of bands. For sure.
